title: Staying Checked In
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Drawing on a Gallup finding that only about 30 percent of teachers are engaged at work, Stuart argues that the human heart disengages when pressure never lets up. His encouraging point is that much of teachers' pressure is self-inflicted, since they agreed to be professionals rather than saviors, and he compares them to doctors who work hard for patients without being omnipotent. He proposes a five-minute walk and two questions about what is weighing on you and how it would look if it were simple. As evidence he describes dropping rubrics and individualized feedback for pop-up debates, replacing them with listening, brief coaching, and whole-class reflection. The move is to treat teacher burnout as something partly within a teacher's control to simplify.
points: Human performance is limited; unrelenting pressure leads educators to disengage or burn out.
Much teacher pressure is self-imposed, because the job is professionalism, not omnipotence.
Two questions on a short walk, what weighs on me and what would simple look like, can reset the load.
Pop-up debates without rubrics or individual feedback worked just as well, showing simpler can be enough.
Teachers have agency over how they think about their work and can act on the pressure they create.
quotes: I use this information to remind colleagues of a thing we forget: human performance is not unlimited. When people experience too much pressure — and nearly all educators do — the human soul wisely disengages. It’s either disengagement or destruction.
The heart cannot indefinitely stay emotionally connected to work that is always screaming, “MORE MORE MORE!” And so it is that only 30% of teachers tend to be engaged in their work.

The good news, of course, is that much of the pressure we feel is self-inflicted. We didn’t sign a contract at the outset that we would be the savior of our students. No — quite differently, we agreed to be professionals.
But the doctor also has enormous agency of whether or not she will become overly pressured. She gets to think about how she thinks about the work.

I used to feel that for every pop-up debate, I needed to have a rubric, and I needed to give each of my students some kind of individualized feedback. Then one day, I decided that I’d forget about those things and just listen to the students during their debate.

We identified an area for improvement today, and I taught a brief mini-lesson on that skill. And then we had another pop-up debate the same way — no rubric, no individualized feedback. Over one hundred pop-up debates later, I’ve not missed rubrics or individualized feedback a single time — and my students haven’t either.
